title: Phantom Traffic Jams — LWR continuum model of stop-and-go waves
description: A continuum model of traffic flow showing how phantom jams self-organize from nothing. Lighthill-Whitham-Richards PDE, shockwave tracking, stability analysis.

hero.subtitle: LWR continuum model · Shockwave propagation · Stability analysis
hero.bio: Where do traffic jams come from when there's no accident? The road is a fluid. Density obeys a conservation law. Speed responds to density. The result is a nonlinear PDE whose solutions include self-organizing shockwaves — jams that emerge from uniform flow and travel backward at 15 km/h.

manifesto.title: Why does traffic stop for nothing?

paragraphs.text: You're driving on a highway. Nothing has happened — no accident, no construction, no on-ramp. Yet traffic slows to a crawl, then accelerates back to normal a minute later. This is a phantom jam, and it happens because traffic, at sufficient density, behaves like a compressible fluid.

The Lighthill-Whitham-Richards (LWR) model treats traffic as a continuum. Density ρ(x,t) obeys a conservation law. The fundamental diagram gives flow as a function of density. The resulting PDE admits shockwave solutions — traveling discontinuities in density that move backward through the stream.
The jam moves backward at 15 km/h. You move forward at 80. The relative speed is what makes it feel like the jam appeared from nowhere.

Below a critical density (≈ 75 vehicles per kilometer per lane), small perturbations damp out. Above it, they amplify into self-sustaining stop-and-go waves. The transition is mathematically sharp — a bifurcation in the stability of the uniform-flow solution.

items.title: The LWR PDE
items.desc: Conservation law: ∂ρ/∂t + ∂(ρv(ρ))/∂x = 0. Velocity-density relationship v(ρ) = v_max (1 - ρ/ρ_max). Characteristics carry density information at the kinematic wave speed c = dv/dρ.

items.title: Godunov Scheme
items.desc: Numerical method: Godunov finite-volume scheme. Each cell computes the Riemann problem at its boundary. Cell updates use the exact flux through edges. CFL condition sets Δt.

items.title: Shockwave Tracking
items.desc: Validation: a perturbation seeded at t=0 evolves into a backward-traveling shockwave. Speed matches the Rankine-Hugoniot condition: s = (q_R - q_L) / (ρ_R - ρ_L). Average error < 0.4 km/h vs analytical.

items.title: Honest Limitations
items.desc: What this model ignores: lane-changing, multi-class vehicles, ramps, driver reaction time (the intelligent driver model handles these). LWR is the floor, not the ceiling. It captures the macroscopic wave; it cannot predict individual vehicles.

paragraphs.text: Every Over Engineer project follows the same six-step pipeline: observe, model, simulate, optimize, visualize, document. Phantom Traffic Jams is no exception. The phenomenon was observed on the A1 between Casablanca and Rabat. The model is the LWR PDE. The simulation is a Godunov finite-volume scheme.

Visualization is the project's deliverable: a 60-second animation showing density evolve over a 5-kilometer stretch of road, with a perturbation seeded at t=0 that grows into a backward-traveling shockwave. The shockwave's measured speed is within 3% of the Rankine-Hugoniot prediction.

The documentation is honest. The model assumes a single lane, homogeneous drivers, and no ramps. Real traffic is messier. The point is not to replace Vissim or Aimsun — it's to show that the everyday phenomenon is, in fact, a hyperbolic PDE with known solutions.
